"Lanky" describes a person who is tall and thin, but in an ungainly, loose-limbed way. It is not just about being tall, and not just about being thin — it is the combination of both, along with a sense that the person's long limbs look a little awkward or loosely put together, like their body hasn't quite caught up with itself.

Think of a teenager who shot up several inches over a summer. Their arms hang a bit too long, their legs look spindly, and they move with a slightly clumsy, uncoordinated quality. That person is lanky.
Breaking it down: the three ingredients

When you call someone lanky, you are really pointing to three things at once:

  1. Tall — they are noticeably above average height.
  2. Thin — they have a slim, narrow build with little bulk or muscle.
  3. Loose or awkward-looking — their long limbs give them a slightly ungainly, poorly-coordinated appearance, as if their arms and legs are just a little too long for the rest of their body.

Remove any one of these and the word no longer fits perfectly. A short, thin person is not lanky. A tall, muscular person is not lanky. A tall, thin person who moves with great grace and elegance is usually not called lanky either.
The feeling of the word — its connotation

"Lanky" is a mildly informal and slightly negative word, though not cruelly so. It is more descriptive than insulting — something you might say affectionately, or casually, rather than as a sharp criticism.

It does carry a quiet implication of awkwardness. There is something a little unfinished or gawky about a lanky person — like a young foal whose legs are too long. It is often associated with adolescence, growth spurts, and that phase when a young person has not yet "grown into" their body.

That said, the word is not harsh. Saying "he is a lanky kid" is very different from saying something unkind. It is simply an honest, informal observation about how someone is built.
How it differs from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so here is a clear breakdown:

  • Slim / slender / lean — These just mean thin, and they are positive or neutral. A slim person looks elegant and well-proportioned. Lanky is different because it adds awkwardness and excessive height.
  • Gaunt — This means extremely thin in an unhealthy, hollow-cheeked way — almost sickly. Lanky does not imply illness; it just describes a tall, thin body type.
  • Gangly / gangling — These are the closest synonyms to lanky. They mean almost exactly the same thing: tall, thin, and awkward-looking. You can use them interchangeably in most sentences. "Gangly" perhaps emphasizes the awkward movement even more, but the difference is tiny.
  • Rangy — Similar again: tall and thin with long limbs. "Rangy" is slightly more neutral and is sometimes used positively (it can suggest athletic potential or a wiry toughness), whereas "lanky" leans more toward awkward.
  • Beanpole / string bean — These are informal or slang expressions for a very tall, thin person. They are more vivid and playful, and a bit more exaggerated.

The word is used almost exclusively for people, and occasionally for animals — a lanky young horse, a lanky dog with long legs.

It is most naturally applied to young people, especially teenagers, because the awkward-growth-spurt quality of the word fits that stage of life so well. But it can describe adults too — someone who has always had a tall, thin, loose-limbed build.

It is rarely (and only metaphorically) applied to objects or things.

• "The lanky teenager had to duck his head every time he walked through a doorway."
  • "She was lanky as a child but grew into a graceful, confident woman."
  • "The new basketball recruit was lanky but showed a lot of promise."
  • "A lanky figure in an oversized coat stood at the corner of the street."
  • "He had the lanky, loose-jointed look of someone who had grown six inches in one year."
Quick summary to lock it in

Lanky = tall + thin + awkward-looking, usually in a harmless, informal, slightly affectionate way. The image to hold in your mind is a young person with long arms, long legs, and a narrow frame — moving through the world in a slightly gawky, uncoordinated way, like their limbs arrived before the rest of them did.
